newsitem.title: USA: Disney buys Mammoth Records to boost music presence.
newsitem.headline: Disney buys Mammoth Records to boost music presence.

text.p: Walt Disney Co. on Monday announced a deal to buy successful independent label Mammoth Records in an effort to boost its image in the music industry.
The Burbank, Calif.-based entertainment giant did not disclose how much it agreed to spend on the alternative rock music label, but industry sources put the price at around $25 million.
"I think it's a step towards giving them critical mass in the music business, making that business much more viable for Disney," said Cowen & Co. analyst Harold Vogel.
Mammoth will be part of a music group that also includes Disney's struggling Hollywood Records and a newly launched Nashville label, all to be distributed by PolyGram NV, the sources said.

Disney has had several setbacks in the music business, including continued troubles at Hollywood Records, which has failed to break any hit acts in its seven-year history and instead incurred about $100 million in losses.

Last month, Hollywood Records faced further embarrassment when it yanked a new album by the rap group Insane Clown Posse just six hours after it hit store shelves because Disney management deemed the album's lyrical content inappropriate.
Since then, Island Records, which is owned by PolyGram, acquired the rights to Insane Clown Posse, which is expected to be a huge seller.

Hollywood Records has been operating without a president since Bob Pfiefer was let go in April and the label failed to lure Tom Whalley, president of the successful Interscope Records label, to head Disney's music operations.
In May, Whalley left Interscope to assume leadership at Hollywood Records, only to announce two days later that he had returned to Interscope.

"Industry executives had questioned why Whalley would want to quit the most successful label to join the most ridiculed," said Tess Taylor, president of the Los Angeles Music Network, an association of record industry professionals.

Industry sources speculated Mammoth founder and President Jay Faires, who entered a five-year employment contract with Disney, is a shoe-in for the top job overseeing all of the music operations, which may be reorganized.

Disney Studios Chairman Joe Roth "may want at sometime to do some consolidation, but at this point, all the labels will operate independently," said a Disney spokesman, adding that Faires will serve as president of Mammoth.

"I've heard that Joe Roth is going to put hundreds of millions of dollars into the music business and if Mammoth does really well, there's a good chance Faires' role will broaden," said a source close to the company.
In an interview, Faires declined to comment on such speculation.
"Joe (Roth) likes to play to win and wants to give more resources (to music) and he's not going to take a half step. He'll back us up," Faires said.

Based in Carrboro, N.C., with offices in New York, Los Angeles and London, Mammoth has a roster of more than 25 artists, including the gold-record-selling Squirrel Nut Zippers as well as Frente!, The Backsliders and Pure.
"We'll be building up the New York and Los Angeles offices. We'll probably hire 15 to 20 people over the next two years," he said. Started by Faires in 1988, Mammoth currently employs 30 people.
Mammoth also has a catalogue of about 120 albums.

In 1995, as part of a previous joint venture, Faires became vice president of artists and repertoire at Time Warner Inc.'s Atlantic Records and signed several artists, including the platinum act Seven Mary Three.
Disney's stock fell 69 cents to $75.19 in consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading.
